item.title: France: Far-right party’s ‘de‑demonisation’ strategy rattled by antisemitism scandal
item.description:
France: Far-right party’s ‘de‑demonisation’ strategy rattled by antisemitism scandal

Submitted by Tassa Adidi on Wed, 10/14/2026 - 08:44
Allegations of antisemitism targeting National Rally president Jordan Bardella have undermined the party’s attempt to move beyond its extremist past
France's far-right Rassemblement National leader Jordan Bardella (R) attends a conference on antisemitism in Jerusalem on 27 March 2025 (Menahem Kahana/AFP)
Off

“Nature always returns,” says the proverb - a phrase that perfectly captures the current predicament of the president of France’s far-right Rassemblement National (RN).

Jordan Bardella is facing serious allegations published by the investigative outlet Mediapart, which attributes to him antisemitic messages exchanged on social networks in 2013, when he was 17 and already a party member.

According to Mediapart, Bardella allegedly wrote on Messenger: “Banks are all owned by Jews,” “The Jew must dominate other peoples, crush them and steal from them; a Zionist is necessarily Jewish, and deeply so,” and “The most important ministries go to people for whom Israel and banking interests take precedence over French interests.”

Bardella, an MEP since 2019, has denied the accusations, denouncing “crude fabrications, obscure and manipulable screenshots reproducing vile statements I obviously never made.” He has filed complaints for defamation, forgery and use of forgery.

RN officials have rallied around him, with Marine Le Pen leading the charge. The party’s candidate for next year’s presidential election said she trusts Bardella “a thousand percent”, accusing Mediapart of a “vile manoeuvre”.

Amid the turmoil, Bardella also received support from an unexpected figure: Amichai Chikli, Israel’s minister in charge of combating antisemitism, who described him as “one of the clearest voices in Europe against Hamas”.

“No one will convince me that Jordan Bardella hates the Jewish people or the Jewish state,” Chikli said.

In 2025, during an International Conference on Combating Antisemitism, the Israeli minister hosted Bardella, who has consistently presented himself as a friend of Jews and Israel.

The event, held in Jerusalem and attended by other European far‑right figures as well as numerous supporters of US President Donald Trump, was boycotted by several European and international Jewish organisations.

From antisemitism to Israeli alignment

In recent years, Israel has drawn closer to several European far‑right parties, united by a shared agenda on security and opposition to Islamist movements.

For French Green MP Sabrina Sebaihi, Israel’s continued support for Bardella despite Mediapart’s revelations stems from the fact that he “supports its genocidal project” in Gaza.

‘The most important thing for the Israeli government is not the fight against antisemitism, but the eradication of the Palestinian people and the occupation of their land’

- Sabrina Sebaihi, Green MP

“The most important thing for the Israeli government is not the fight against antisemitism, but the eradication of the Palestinian people and the occupation of their land,” she told Middle East Eye.

She pointed to “an alliance of convenience” between Israel and the RN, recalling that the party was founded by members of the Waffen‑SS, the armed military units of the Nazi.

Before changing its name in 2018, the RN was called the Front National (FN). The FN was founded by Jean-Marie Le Pen, Marine Le Pen’s father, along with members of various far-right movements, including Pierre Bousquet and Leon Gaultier, both former Waffen-SS, and supporters of French Algeria.

Jean‑Marie Le Pen himself had been a lieutenant in a paratrooper regiment during the French colonisation of Algeria, where he allegedly tortured independence activists. A notorious antisemite, he once declared that gas chambers in Nazi concentration camps were “a detail of history”.

Despite Le Pen’s record and six criminal convictions, Bardella defended him in 2023, even denying that he was antisemitic. He later paid tribute to the former FN leader after his death in 2025. A widely shared photograph also shows an 18‑year‑old Bardella waiting in line to meet Le Pen, whom he regarded as a key figure of the movement.

At the time, Bardella also associated with members of the Group Union Defense (GUD), a violent far-right student group, and with one of its former members, Frederic Chatillon, a close associate of Marine Le Pen.

Mediapart also attributes to Bardella a fascination with Alain Soral, a Holocaust‑denying polemicist repeatedly convicted by French courts. “His analyses are accurate because everything is confirmed by the facts,” Bardella allegedly wrote.

Jean-Marie Le Pen, who brought French far right into the mainstream, dies at 96
Read More »

Close to Jean-Marie Le Pen, Soral joined the party’s central committee in 2007. But Marine Le Pen pushed him out two years later as part of her so-called “de-demonisation” strategy.

The goal of this policy, which became the goal of Marine Le Pen’s leadership, was to shed the party’s image as a radical far-right movement and break its association with antisemitism, seen as a major obstacle to electoral success.

This involved removing candidates who displayed racist, antisemitic, homophobic or neo-Nazi messages, and even excluding the party’s founder - her own father - in 2015 over his antisemitic and Holocaust-denying remarks.

Marine Le Pen chose to form a duo with Bardella, encouraging his rise to the RN presidency to present a youthful, suit-and-tie image far removed from the party’s historical far-right figures.

Elected RN president in 2022 at age 27, Bardella became a pillar of the party’s de-demonisation strategy. Gone were the provocations and scandals: the RN sought to appear as a moderate, respectable party ready to govern, presenting itself as a bulwark against antisemitism while embracing an overtly pro‑Israel stance.

Cosmetic change

However, experts on the party argue that the strategy is primarily a media smoothing operation. Historian and political scientist Sylvain Boulouque explains that this “facade of normalisation” does not alter the party’s deep ideological foundations.

“Despite the change in rhetoric, the RN’s core programme - national preference, sovereignty, opposition to immigration, identity politics, hardline security - remains rooted in the historical identity of the far right,” he told MEE.

‘Antisemitism is a founding dimension of the far right and has never disappeared’

- Sylvain Boulouque, historian and political scientist

“Antisemitism is a founding dimension of the far right and has never disappeared,” Boulouque added. “A portion of the RN electorate fully identifies with the statements attributed to Bardella,” he said.

Outraged by the Mediapart revelations, Sebaihi took the matter to court. Backed by a dozen left‑wing MPs, she announced plans to refer the case to the Paris public prosecutor. In a letter seen by AFP, she cited facts “likely to receive criminal qualification due to their antisemitic nature”.

“It is our duty as political leaders to never let antisemitic, Islamophobic, racist or xenophobic statements go unchallenged. The lack of systematic condemnation of such remarks contributes to the liberation of racist speech and deepens fractures in our country,” she said.

Sebaihi argues that the messages attributed to Bardella show that the RN’s de-demonisation is a sham.

“They changed the shop window, but the core of this party remains the same - fundamentally racist and antisemitic,” the MP told MEE.

The president of the Representative Council of Jewish Institutions of France (CRIF), Yonathan Arfi, also notes that “antisemitism remains widespread among RN supporters and even among its officials”. “It seems illusory to believe that the RN could protect Jews,” he added.

In a column published in Le Monde, Judith Cohen Solal, a psychoanalyst, and Jonathan Hayoun, a documentarist, recall that the far right’s deep DNA is structured around hatred of Jews.

‘Policing thought’: French bill to fight antisemitism accused of silencing Israel critics
Read More »

“The man who walked through Jerusalem in March 2025 claiming that ‘the fight against antisemitism must tolerate no ambiguity’, the man meant to embody the very face of de-demonisation, is today caught up by his own antisemitic writings,” they wrote.

In 2019, they published a book showing how far‑right leaders like Marine Le Pen and Bardella seized on the rise of violent militant groups such as the Islamic State to court a previously hostile Jewish electorate, framing Muslims - or “Islamism” - as “the real antisemites”.

The narrative helped the RN appear more respectable while deepening hostility toward Muslims.

But this philosemitic posture, which the RN embraced more strongly after 7 October, has not fooled observers. Cohen Solal told MEE that the party sought to shed its antisemitic image solely to expand its electoral base.

“There has been no work of repair or reflection on antisemitism within the RN,” she said, adding that Mediapart’s revelations “support the arguments of those who were already convinced” of the party’s antisemitic nature.

Will these revelations harm the RN ahead of the 2027 presidential election? Cohen Solal does not think so: “We can see that Bardella denies the facts and his supporters back him, crying conspiracy.”

For his part, Boulouque notes that studies show the RN’s electoral base is antisemitic.

According to a recent poll, only 45 percent of RN voters consider the antisemitic statements attributed to Bardella “serious”, compared to 74 percent for the general population and approximately 95 percent on the left and centre of the political spectrum.

Meanwhile, despite a slight drop in popularity this month (-4 points), Bardella remains, alongside Le Pen, one of the frontrunners in polls for the presidential race.

item.title: France is on the precipice of a far-right landslide
item.description:
France is on the precipice of a far-right landslide

Submitted by Rayan Freschi on Wed, 10/07/2026 - 21:08
Presidential frontrunner Marine Le Pen's hijab obsession is merely a symptom of the country's deeply rooted Islamophobia
National Rally leader Marine Le Pen speaks during a party rally in Chalons-en-Champagne, France, on 18 March 2026 (Sameer al-Doumy/AFP)
Off

The French presidential race has begun. For the first time since 2017, Emmanuel Macron won’t be a part of it. 

And for the first time in her career, Marine Le Pen is the clear frontrunner, even after her conviction in a corruption scandal almost prevented her from running for public office.

Prior to the final ruling, her second-in-command, Jordan Bardella, had tried to force his way in as the strongest National Rally presidential candidate, believing that Le Pen’s judicial vulnerability might translate an into electoral one - a costly ambition for which he is now paying, after Le Pen fired his closest associates inside the party.

Now fully at her mercy, he may even lose his position as the movement’s president to Le Pen’s nephew, Marion Marechal, whose politics are even more racist than his own. 

The outcome of this troubled political-judicial sequence is not only Le Pen’s renewed control over her troops, and the expectation that she will win the first round of voting. Polls also identify her as the favourite for the second round, regardless of her rival.

In short, the 2027 race is widely believed to be Le Pen’s to lose, after she launched her campaign around the themes of immigration and Islam. 

She plans to hold two referendums: one asking whether the French population supports her plan to restrict immigration, and another on banning the hijab in public spaces. Both would seek to cement the legitimacy of structural racism and Islamophobia through majoritarian approval. 

Bleak landscape

Similar to the tactics used by Reform UK leader Nigel Farage with regards to Brexit, Le Pen knows how effective a well-organised and relentless campaign can be. 

When mainstream media bombards the public with a specific narrative - even a false one - the Overton window can be drastically expanded across a bleak political landscape.

Encouraged by their victories in the Islamophobic culture wars that have shaped the West since 9/11, and by the recent electoral coronations of US President Donald Trump, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and Germany’s AfD, French fascists believe they are on the verge of reaching the mountaintop. 

We are witnessing not an event, but an epoch. The eventual rise to power of the National Rally would be one of its chapters

France - like the US, Italy and Germany before it - is ripe for a final and decisive push.

To paraphrase philosopher Antonio Gramsci, we are witnessing not an event, but an epoch. The eventual rise to power of the National Rally would be one of its chapters. 

This epoch began with the US invasion of Afghanistan in 2001, and the forces at play today are the mature offspring of that “war on terror”. While these movements refuse to hide their supremacist nature and authoritarian intent behind a veneer of political decorum, they do not fundamentally differ at their core from the governments that preceded them; they merely call for draconian Islamophobic measures to be adopted faster, with the backing of entire societies. 

The proposed hijab referendum in France should not be understood only as the move of an obsessively Islamophobic party, nostalgic for its colonial past. More broadly, it offers a perfect opportunity for an obsessively Islamophobic nation, nostalgic for its colonial past, to adopt legislation that could drive the last nail into the coffin of Muslims’ freedom of religion.

Cynical tactics

The electoral chessboard seems to offer only one surprising option for Muslims: Jean-Luc Melenchon, head of the far-left France Unbowed party. It’s surprising because over the last two decades, Melenchon has been at the forefront of French Islamophobia. 

He endorsed the 2004 ban on the hijab in public schools, and years later supported the niqab ban, referring to veiled Muslim women as “ghosts”. He was also a staunch supporter of Bashar al-Assad at the height of the Syrian civil war, despite the former president’s crimes against the Syrian people. 

But amid Israel’s genocide in Gaza, Melenchon seemed to take a step towards the Muslim community. His party was the only one to firmly oppose Israel’s actions, even backing a Palestinian candidate, Rima Hassan, for the European Parliament. 

Why is France so obsessed with controlling Muslim women's bodies?
Read More »

From 2023 onwards, just a year after his disappointing defeat in the last presidential election, Melenchon’s pro-Palestinian stance gave his party much-needed momentum at a moment when his political career was on the line, breathing new life into his presidential ambitions.

His recent apology for his previous opposition to the hijab, which he called a “terrible mistake”, suggested that he might have finally come to his senses on the urgent matter of Muslim freedom of religion. But he has also reportedly promised not to repeal the 2004 ban, to avoid reopening “the debate about clothing”, and because schools are meant to “protect children”.

This contradiction can easily be explained by the cynical calculations of electoral politics. Confident that his position will secure him enough Muslim votes to reach the second round, Melenchon is preparing to then challenge Le Pen on her own turf, and potentially win over some of her voters. 

Structural Islamophobia would still have a bright future under his leadership, as he is clearly reluctant to tackle the nation’s Islamophobic consensus for the sake of electability. His strategy appears to entail leveraging Muslim grievances to improve his chances in the first round, only to abandon them in the second round (and, if successful, once in power).

It is now incumbent on French Muslims to lead a new generation of citizens raging against educational decay and police violence, as well as the atrocities of the “war on terror” and the genocide in Gaza.

item.title: Why did the Palestinian Authority postpone elections - again?
item.description:
Why did the Palestinian Authority postpone elections - again?

Submitted by Lubna Masarwa on Tue, 10/13/2026 - 13:44
A Hamas-Dahlan alliance threatened Fatah's electoral plans and exposed a wider struggle over Palestinian politics
Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas attends the foundation stone ceremony of the Innovation and Excellence Compound in the West Bank city of Ramallah, on 9 September 2026 (Zain Jaafar/AFP)
Off

Three months after Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas announced elections, the vote has been postponed once again, deepening questions over the legitimacy of the Palestinian Authority (PA).

Announced by presidential decree on 10 October, the decision cited Israeli restrictions on the electoral commission and deteriorating conditions in Gaza and the occupied West Bank.

But analysts and Palestinian political insiders say logistical obstacles tell only part of the story.

An unlikely alliance between Hamas and the faction of former Fatah official Mohammed Dahlan, both rivals of Abbas, threatened to upend Fatah’s electoral calculations and challenge its dominance.

The proposed coalition sought to unite major opposition forces and independent figures under one umbrella. 

Its announcement last month prompted a flurry of meetings in Cairo between Fatah, Hamas, Dahlan's faction, and other Palestinian groups.

The talks helped pave the way for postponing the elections from 27 November 2026 to 11 September 2027.

Jibril Rajoub, a senior Fatah official, said earlier this month that the factions would instead prepare for a "comprehensive national dialogue" aimed at reaching "common ground" on political issues before next year’s vote.

But behind the language of consensus lies a deeper struggle over who will shape Palestinian politics, as Abbas faces mounting pressure, while the emerging alliance threatens to redraw the political map.

Calculations

The last Palestinian parliamentary elections were held in 2006, when Hamas won a surprise majority over Fatah, which had long dominated Palestinian politics.

Fighting between the two factions in 2007 led to the emergence of rival administrations: Hamas in Gaza and Fatah in the West Bank.

Repeated attempts at reconciliation and fresh elections have failed for 20 years, leaving Abbas to govern without a renewed electoral mandate.

A senior Fatah insider, who spoke to Middle East Eye on condition of anonymity, said Abbas announced the elections in July largely in response to international pressure to renew the PA's legitimacy.

"Most of our Palestinian elections take place under external pressure," the insider said, pointing to European pressure and reform commitments Abbas had reportedly made to France.

The timing, however, appeared disconnected from conditions on the ground.

Gaza remained devastated by Israel's genocide in the enclave, with Palestinians struggling to secure food and shelter. In the occupied West Bank, Palestinians face a worsening economic crisis, escalating Israeli settler violence and tighter movement restrictions.

Can Palestinian elections still matter after the Gaza genocide?
Read More »

"The announcement of the elections was surprising and incomprehensible to the Palestinian people," the insider said.

"People in Gaza cannot find food or a place to live, and people talk about elections. I do not think this was an appropriate time for it."

Hani al-Masri, a Palestinian political analyst, said the timing also reflected a calculation in Ramallah that Hamas had been weakened by Israel's genocide in Gaza, creating an opening for Fatah to regain ground.

But those calculations became increasingly uncertain.

Hamas quickly welcomed the election announcement and declared its intention to participate as part of the broadest possible coalition.

A month later, it announced an alliance involving Dahlan’s faction - a striking development given his history as a bitter rival of the group and his close ties to the United Arab Emirates (UAE).

"The coalition had yet taken its final shape, but the mere fact that its idea emerged had the impact of a thunderbolt on the PA's leadership," Masri said.

"Initially, there was talk that the coalition would bring in major political forces and prominent individuals, which would be able to win a majority of the seats and change the political landscape."

Masri said opinion polls had continued to show declining support for Fatah and Abbas, driven by internal divisions, corruption allegations, economic hardship, and mounting public anger.

Against this backdrop, the PA pushed the elections back by nearly a year.

But Masri believes the Hamas-Dahlan alliance is unlikely to disappear.

From enemies to partners

A longtime Fatah member, Dahlan headed the Preventive Security Force in Gaza after the PA was established under the Oslo Accords in the 1990s.

As head of the force, he oversaw crackdowns, arrests and the suppression of Hamas members.

After Hamas won the 2006 elections, it accused Dahlan of plotting a coup. The ensuing infighting ended with Dahlan being driven out of Gaza by force.

He later fell out with Abbas and went into self-imposed exile in the UAE, where he maintains close ties with the country’s rulers.

His new alignment with Hamas has therefore surprised many Palestinians.

'Hamas needed someone to help it climb down from the tree'

- Hani al-Masri, a political analyst

But according to Masri, cooperation between the two sides did not emerge overnight. He said contacts over financial assistance to Gaza had been active as far back as 2017.

Their cooperation intensified after Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza began in 2023, with Dahlan becoming a key figure in bringing in aid, facilitating social initiatives and establishing political contacts.

"The money comes from the UAE, but it’s facilitated by Dahlan," the Fatah insider said.

He argued that Dahlan’s role in channelling assistance helped boost his popularity and made a return to Palestinian politics increasingly plausible.

Another factor, he said, was the current PA leadership's poor performance.

"People think, well, if not Mohammed Dahlan, then who?" he said.

The insider also pointed to Dahlan's role in backchannel talks with the US over a ceasefire agreement in Gaza.

Palestinian elites have been collaborating against the resistance for a century
Read More »

Hamas, meanwhile, has emerged from the war in a difficult financial and political position, helping explain its willingness to work with a former adversary.

"Hamas needed someone to help it climb down from the tree," Masri said. 

The alliance, he argued, could mark the beginning of a new political order. But he warned that it risked taking shape without a coherent national programme.

"There is a new [political] map taking shape, but it doesn’t have a national programme," he said.

He argued that any new leadership must address the immediate needs of Palestinians across Gaza and the occupied West Bank while preserving a broader political project.

"It is as though, now, in exchange for a loaf of bread and medicine, we are willing to give up many things," he said.
